title: Sampling Maps
text:
Goals
What follows is our workflow for generating a figure depicting the sampling localities for all the individual samples included in the Zosterops single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) dataset generated from a double digest restriction-site associated DNA (ddRAD) library (see DeRaad et al.2024 for details on the ddRAD library (DeRaad et al. 2024).

title: Sampling Maps
text:
Getting started
We are using R version 4.4.2, RStudio version 2024.09.1 for the analysis. Quarto version 1.6.39 for Mac OS was used to document the workflow. Set the working directory in RStudio to one where the .txt file denoting the identity and sampling location of the samples are accessible.

title: Sampling Maps
text:
Data files
This analysis requires the following data files.

ZosteropsPOPS4_LatLong.txt A text file of individual samples included in the SNP dataset matched with taxon, locale, and latitude and longitude.
ZosteropsPOPS_SANGER_LatLong.txt A text file of individual samples included in the Sanger sequencing dataset but that do not appear in the SNP dataset matched with taxon, locale, and latitude and longitude.


Individual samples and collecting localities: SNPs
A tab delimited text file with the individual sample IDs, taxon designations, the name of the sampling locales (designated by island or province), and latitude and longitude was created to generate maps. The reduce the amount of clutter on the maps subspecies were clustered together in shared geographic groups. Zosterops japonicus subspecies were designated as either Z. japonicus alani for the most remote subspecies in the Volcano Islands or grouped within a single Z. japonicus designation for all the remaining subspecies. Subspecies for Z. montanus were clustered into three groups including a Palawan group (montanus PALAWAN) consiting of Z. montanus parkesi, a northern Philippine group (montanus NORTH) for those subspecies on Mindoro and Luzon (Z. montanus halconensis amd Z. montanus whiteheadi), and a southern Philippine group (montanus SOUTH) including the remaining Z. montanus subspecies included in the study (Z. montanus diuatae, Z. montanus montanus, Z. montanus pectoralis, Z. montanus vulcani, and an unnamed but suggested subspecies on Panay). Subspecies within the Z. everetti and Z. nigrorum species were lumped together under a single species designation for the sampling maps but distinguished in later analyses. Samples from introduced populations in Hawaii and California are included in this list for completeness as they appear in the SNP dataset, but they are excluded from the final figure. Installing packages and loading libraries
Set the working directory to one where the data files ZosteropsPOPS4_LatLong.txt and Zosterops_SANGER_LatLong.txt are accessible. Creating the sampling maps requires the following R packages.

logr (Bosak 2024) Optional if you wish to create a log file for the analysis.
ggplot2 (Wickham 2016)
maps (Becker, Minka, and Deckmyn. 2024)
sf (Pebesma and Bivand 2023)

Install the packages using the Tools/Install Packages selection from the RStudio menu and load the package libraries.

library(logr)

title: Sampling Maps
section: Read and edit data: SNP sampling
text:
Read and edit data: SNP sampling
Read the data into a data frame using read.csv and indicate that the fields are tab delimited (sep = "\t") and contain a header row (header = TRUE). First complete this process for the sampling data for teh SNP dataset.

# Read tab delimited (sep = "\t") file with latitude and longitude
ZLocations <- read.csv("Data/Location files/ZosteropsPOPS4_LatLong.txt", sep = "\t", header = TRUE)

Remove the samples from the introduced populations. Those samples are from Los Angeles (Z. simplex) and Hawaii (Z. japonicus) and are included in analyses but will not appear on the sampling maps. We can assume readers know where Hawaii and Los Angeles are.

# Remove Los Angeles and Hawaii samples
ZLocations_NATIVE <- ZLocations[-c(105,106,107,120,121,122,123,124),]

title: Sampling Maps
section: Count individual samples per taxon: SNP sampling
text:
Count individual samples per taxon: SNP sampling
To illustrate the relative number of individual samples from any particular site we will count the number of samples associated with a unique latitude and longitude. First split the data frame by the TAXON column.

# Split by TAXON
Zlocations_NATIVE_TAXON <- split(ZLocations_NATIVE, ZLocations_NATIVE$TAXON)

Using a loop count samples grouped by LAT and LONG columns and save this as a new data frame called sampling.df.

#init sampling.df which will be a df of samples grouped by unique lat/long
sampling.df<-data.frame(NULL)
#use a for loop to split the dataframe by species and summarize the number of individuals sampled at each locality for each species
for (i in names(Zlocations_NATIVE_TAXON)){
  samps <- Zlocations_NATIVE_TAXON[[i]] %>% dplyr::group_by(LAT, LONG) %>% dplyr::summarize(count=dplyr::n())
  df <- cbind(rep(i, times=nrow(samps)), samps)
  sampling.df <- as.data.frame(rbind(sampling.df, df))
}

title: Sampling Maps
text:
Create a sampling map

Mapping all samples
Download a world base map.

#make base world map
pac<-map_data("world")

First create a sampling map for all the Zosterops samples in the study (excluding those from introduced populations). Include two lines with the geo_point command. One line will define those points from the SNP sampling data frame (sampling.df) and will define those points as filled circles (pch=21). The next line will define the points using the geo_point command for the additional Sanger sequencing samples (samplingSANGER.df) and define those points as triangles (pch=24). Because many of the sampling locations are the same for different taxa define position = position_jitter(h=0.5, w=0.5) to offset the points on the map so as they do not perfectly overlap. Also set alpha=0.5 to make the points transparent. This will also help in showing those places where sampled taxa overlap in location.

# plot all native samples
ggplot()+

title: Distance trees, PCA, and DAPC analyses
text:
What follows is an analysis of the Zosterops single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) data from our double digest restriction-site associated DNA (ddRAD) library. This analysis seeks to describe general metrics of diversity and variation in East Asian Zosterops and makes some attempt to assess the utility of these data in clustering individuals by putative taxonomic and population groups.



We are using R version 4.4.2, RStudio version 2024.09.1 for the analysis. Quarto version 1.6.39 for Mac OS was used to document the workflow. Set the working directory in RStudio to one where the .vcf.gz zipped data file and a .txt file denoting the identity of the samples are accessible.



This analysis requires the following data files.

zost.filtered.snps.vcf.gz The gzipped file containing the filtered SNP data in variant call format (VCF) (see DeRaad et al. 2024 for details on creation of the ddRAD library and filtering the SNP dataset) (DeRaad et al. 2024)
ZosteropsPOPS4.txt The text file containing the taxon and locale data for each individual sample in the SNP dataset.

Discriminant analysis of principal components (DAPC) is a multivariate method that takes principal components (PCs) and partitions variance into within- and among-group components in a way that maximizes discrimination among the groups (Thibaut Jombart, Devillard, and Balloux 2010). DAPC makes no explicit assumptions regarding recombination or panmixia. This allows us use of the full SNP dataset without worrying about filtering to reduce the likelihood of linkage as is required for STRUCTURE or ADMIXTURE. An excellent tutorial on DAPC is available here. First conduct a cross-validation analysis to help determine the optimal number of PCs to be retained in the DAPC. Test between 1 and 50 PCs (n.pca = 1:50) with 100 replicate runs per PC (n.rep = 100) of the cross-validation analysis. Use the multicore option and 6 CPUs (ncpus = 6L), potentially more if your machine allows it. Even running multiple cores this run can take a while to execute. Executing this analysis within the system.time command will return an elapsed time for the operation. This will return a graph showing the proportion of successful group predictions on the y-axis and the results from the individual replicate runs for each PC on the x-axis.

library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

The DAPC cross validation provides some clues as to where we no longer need to add PCs to the DAPC to get increased discrimination, but we want to know exactly how many PCs is optimum for discrimination. The a-score is the difference between the proportion of successful reassignments using the real groups and assignments into randomly assigned groups. Thus the average a-score is the average percent improvement in discrimination over that based on random groupings. The code below will estimate the a-score across 30 replicate runs (n.sim = 30) and 40 PCs (n.pca = 40) showing the result per group for each run, the average across all replicates per group, and the overall average.

ZosteropsSNPsDAPC_OPTIMUM <- dapc(gl.ZosteropsSNPs, n.pca = 40, n.da = nPop(gl.ZosteropsSNPs)-1)
a.score(ZosteropsSNPsDAPC_OPTIMUM, n.pca = 1:ncol(ZosteropsSNPsDAPC_OPTIMUM$tab), n=30, plot = FALSE, n.sim = 30)

Conduct the final DAPC analysis with group assignments for each individual sample. Three runs will be repeated for this analysis. One of those runs uses the optimal number of PCs from the prior iterated a-score estimations (the median optimal number of PCs across 100 replicate runs of the optimal a-score estimation) and the other two runs of the DAPC analysis are four PCs less than the optimal and four PCs greater than the optimal number of PCs. Generate a scatter plot from the DAPC analysis and a bar plot showing the probability of assignment for each individual sample. Save both the scatter plot and bar graphs as pdfs and generate a tab delimited table of the results with the columns being the original assigned population, the sample, the population assigned by the DAPC, and the posterior probability of that particular assignment. In addition, for each replicate run generate a loading plot displaying how each SNP contributes to the PCs for the optimal number of PCs and four less than and four greater than the optimal number. Export each loading plot as a pdf.

n.pca.values <- c(4, 8, 12)
for (n.pca in n.pca.values) {
  DAPCseed = sample(1:999, 1)
  print(DAPCseed)
  set.seed(DAPCseed)
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPC <- dapc(gl.ZosteropsSNPs, n.pca = n.pca, n.da = nPop(gl.ZosteropsSNPs)-1)
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPC_contributions <- loadingplot(ZosteropsSNPsDAPC$var.contr, axis = 2, thres = 0.0025, lab.jitter = 1)
  DAPCscatter <- scatter(ZosteropsSNPsDAPC, col = ColorPal_CUSTOM, cex = 3, legend = TRUE, clabel = F, posi.leg = "bottomleft", scree.pca = TRUE,
          posi.pca = "topright", cleg = 0.75)
  DAPCscatter
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults <- as.data.frame(ZosteropsSNPsDAPC$posterior)
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults$pop <- pop(gl.ZosteropsSNPs)
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults$indNames <- rownames(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults)
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults <- pivot_longer(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults, -c(pop, indNames))
  head(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults, n = 11)
  nPCAtitle <- paste(n.pca, "principal components")
  print(nPCAtitle)
  colnames(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults) <- c("Original_Pop","Sample","Assigned_Pop","Posterior_membership_probability")
  DAPCbar <- ggplot(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults, aes(x=Sample, y=Posterior_membership_probability, fill=Assigned_Pop))
  DAPCbar <-  DAPCbar + geom_bar(stat='identity') 
  DAPCbar <-  DAPCbar + ggtitle(nPCAtitle)
  DAPCbar <-  DAPCbar + scale_fill_manual(values = ColorPal_CUSTOM) 
  DAPCbar <-  DAPCbar + facet_grid(~Original_Pop, scales = "free")
  DAPCbar <-  DAPCbar + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, size = 8))
  print(DAPCbar)
  write.table(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults, file = paste("ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults","_",n.pca,"PCs.txt"), row.names = FALSE, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE)
}

title: Distance trees, PCA, and DAPC analyses
text: What follows is an analysis of the Zosterops single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) data from our double digest restriction-site associated DNA (ddRAD) library. This analysis seeks to describe general metrics of diversity and variation in East Asian Zosterops and makes some attempt to assess the utility of these data in clustering individuals by putative taxonomic and population groups.

title: Distance trees, PCA, and DAPC analyses
text: We are using R version 4.4.2, RStudio version 2024.09.1 for the analysis. Quarto version 1.6.39 for Mac OS was used to document the workflow. Set the working directory in RStudio to one where the .vcf.gz zipped data file and a .txt file denoting the identity of the samples are accessible.

title: Distance trees, PCA, and DAPC analyses
text:

zost.filtered.snps.vcf.gz The gzipped file containing the filtered SNP data in variant call format (VCF) (see DeRaad et al. 2024 for details on creation of the ddRAD library and filtering the SNP dataset) (DeRaad et al. 2024)
ZosteropsPOPS4.txt The text file containing the taxon and locale data for each individual sample in the SNP dataset.

title: Distance trees, PCA, and DAPC analyses
text:
Discriminant analysis of principal components (DAPC) is a multivariate method that takes principal components (PCs) and partitions variance into within- and among-group components in a way that maximizes discrimination among the groups (Thibaut Jombart, Devillard, and Balloux 2010). DAPC makes no explicit assumptions regarding recombination or panmixia. This allows us use of the full SNP dataset without worrying about filtering to reduce the likelihood of linkage as is required for STRUCTURE or ADMIXTURE. An excellent tutorial on DAPC is available here. First conduct a cross-validation analysis to help determine the optimal number of PCs to be retained in the DAPC. Test between 1 and 50 PCs (n.pca = 1:50) with 100 replicate runs per PC (n.rep = 100) of the cross-validation analysis. Use the multicore option and 6 CPUs (ncpus = 6L), potentially more if your machine allows it. Even running multiple cores this run can take a while to execute. Executing this analysis within the system.time command will return an elapsed time for the operation. This will return a graph showing the proportion of successful group predictions on the y-axis and the results from the individual replicate runs for each PC on the x-axis.

library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

The DAPC cross validation provides some clues as to where we no longer need to add PCs to the DAPC to get increased discrimination, but we want to know exactly how many PCs is optimum for discrimination. The a-score is the difference between the proportion of successful reassignments using the real groups and assignments into randomly assigned groups. Thus the average a-score is the average percent improvement in discrimination over that based on random groupings. The code below will estimate the a-score across 30 replicate runs (n.sim = 30) and 40 PCs (n.pca = 40) showing the result per group for each run, the average across all replicates per group, and the overall average.

ZosteropsSNPsDAPC_OPTIMUM <- dapc(gl.ZosteropsSNPs, n.pca = 40, n.da = nPop(gl.ZosteropsSNPs)-1)
a.score(ZosteropsSNPsDAPC_OPTIMUM, n.pca = 1:ncol(ZosteropsSNPsDAPC_OPTIMUM$tab), n=30, plot = FALSE, n.sim = 30)

Conduct the final DAPC analysis with group assignments for each individual sample. Three runs will be repeated for this analysis. One of those runs uses the optimal number of PCs from the prior iterated a-score estimations (the median optimal number of PCs across 100 replicate runs of the optimal a-score estimation) and the other two runs of the DAPC analysis are four PCs less than the optimal and four PCs greater than the optimal number of PCs. Generate a scatter plot from the DAPC analysis and a bar plot showing the probability of assignment for each individual sample. Save both the scatter plot and bar graphs as pdfs and generate a tab delimited table of the results with the columns being the original assigned population, the sample, the population assigned by the DAPC, and the posterior probability of that particular assignment. In addition, for each replicate run generate a loading plot displaying how each SNP contributes to the PCs for the optimal number of PCs and four less than and four greater than the optimal number. Export each loading plot as a pdf.

n.pca.values <- c(4, 8, 12)
for (n.pca in n.pca.values) {
  DAPCseed = sample(1:999, 1)
  print(DAPCseed)
  set.seed(DAPCseed)
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPC <- dapc(gl.ZosteropsSNPs, n.pca = n.pca, n.da = nPop(gl.ZosteropsSNPs)-1)
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPC_contributions <- loadingplot(ZosteropsSNPsDAPC$var.contr, axis = 2, thres = 0.0025, lab.jitter = 1)
  DAPCscatter <- scatter(ZosteropsSNPsDAPC, col = ColorPal_CUSTOM, cex = 3, legend = TRUE, clabel = F, posi.leg = "bottomleft", scree.pca = TRUE,
          posi.pca = "topright", cleg = 0.75)
  DAPCscatter
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults <- as.data.frame(ZosteropsSNPsDAPC$posterior)
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults$pop <- pop(gl.ZosteropsSNPs)
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults$indNames <- rownames(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults)
  ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults <- pivot_longer(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults, -c(pop, indNames))
  head(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults, n = 11)
  nPCAtitle <- paste(n.pca, "principal components")
  print(nPCAtitle)
  colnames(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults) <- c("Original_Pop","Sample","Assigned_Pop","Posterior_membership_probability")
  DAPCbar <- ggplot(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults, aes(x=Sample, y=Posterior_membership_probability, fill=Assigned_Pop))
  DAPCbar <-  DAPCbar + geom_bar(stat='identity') 
  DAPCbar <-  DAPCbar + ggtitle(nPCAtitle)
  DAPCbar <-  DAPCbar + scale_fill_manual(values = ColorPal_CUSTOM) 
  DAPCbar <-  DAPCbar + facet_grid(~Original_Pop, scales = "free")
  DAPCbar <-  DAPCbar + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, size = 8))
  print(DAPCbar)
  write.table(ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults, file = paste("ZosteropsSNPsDAPCResults","_",n.pca,"PCs.txt"), row.names = FALSE, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE)
}

title: Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees
text:
Goals
What follows is our workflow for the general descriptive analysis of the Sanger sequencing data set for Zosterops. In this analysis we will describe the variation across our individual Sanger sequenced loci and construct trees for each of these loci using distance-based and maximum likelihood methods.

title: Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees
text:
Getting started
We are using R version 4.4.2, RStudio version 2024.09.1 for the analysis. Quarto version 1.6.39 for Mac OS was used to document the workflow. Set the working directory in RStudio to one where the necessary phased Sanger sequencing alignments and other data are accessible.

title: Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees
text:
Data files
This dataset includes Sanger sequenced polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplicon alignments for two mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and six protein coding nuclear loci (cdDNA). Prior to this analysis Sanger sequencing .ab1 files were uploaded to GeneiousⓇ 8.1.9 for editing, alignment, and quality control. Multiple sequencing runs for each amplicon were assembled and assembled loci were aligned across individual samples using Geneious Alignment. Alignments for each locus were trimmed and edited in Geneious and the identity of each locus confirmed with a megablast search. The reading frame was set by eye by avoiding frames with stop codons and a blastp search was done on the translation consensus for each alignment to confirm the locus identity. Alignments were exported as .fasta files.
Phase alignments of diploid cdDNA loci using PHASE 2.1.1 (Stephens, Smith, and Donnelly 2001). First, convert the alignment .fasta files from Geneious to the .inp format for PHASE 2.1.1 using the online SeqPHASE tool (Flot 2009). At the ‘Genotypes to be phased’ prompt click the ‘Browse’ button and select the appropriate .fasta alignment. Click the ‘Run SeqPHASE’ button. Once step 1 of the SeqPHASE process is completed retain the seqphase.const file in addition to the seqphase.inp file and rename each file appropriately to match the locus name (e.g. B3GNT9_seqphase.inp and B3GNT9_seqphase.const for locus B3GNT9).
Move the .inp from SeqPHASE to the directory with PHASE 2.1.1 and cd to that directory in the terminal. The .inp file is used to run the following PHASE 2.1.1 command in the terminal. For each locus <numberseed> should be replaced with an arbitrary number selected by the user and LOCUSNAME replaced with the designated name for that particular locus. Because each locus is relatively short chose the S option at the modeling flag (-M) as it assumes no within-locus recombination. Additional parameters are explained in the documentation for PHASE 2.1.1 available here.
./PHASE -MS -d1 -S<numberseed> -p0.85 -q0.85 -x5 -X10 LOCUSNAME_seqphase.inp LOCUSNAME_seqphase.out 5000 2 500 
Further analysis will require FASTA alignments for each locus where each diploid individual contains two sequences corresponding to each of the two phased alleles determined in PHASE 2.1.1. Return to the online SeqPHASE tool and click the link to ‘step 2’. Select the appropriate .out file generated by the PHASE 2.1.1 run along with the matching .const file generated from step 1 in the SeqPHASE tool where prompted by a ‘Browse…’ button. The ‘Sort sequence’ box should be checked but the ‘Reduce sequences’ box should not be checked. Click the ‘Run SeqPHASE’ button and SeqPHASE will return a .fasta file with the complete sequence alignment and two phased haplotypes designated by the project number for that individual sample followed by a and b respectively. Click the ‘Click here to download the generated Fasta file’ link at the bottom of the page and rename the file to match the locus name. Including the .const file and unchecking the ‘Reduced sequences’ box will ensure the resulting FASTA file includes the full length of the alignment, not just the variable sites.
The phasing procedure was repeated for the following cdDNA FASTA alignments.

B3GNT9.fasta
BIRC2.fasta
CCDC.fasta
GPRC6.fasta
LACTBL.fasta
USP38.fasta

Subsequent analysis requires the following data files including those phased cdDNA alignments from the procedure described above.

Number of sequences
Calculate the number of sequences in the alignment. Diploid phased cdDNA loci will have two sequences per individual sample and haploid mtDNA loci will have a single sequence per locus.

# Number of sequences calulated two ways, by divdiding the total length by the sequence length (calculation 1) and by extracting the length value from the summary (caclulation 2)
# Confirm both calculations for number of sequences are the same
NumberSequencesCOI1 <- lengthCOItotal/seqlengthCOI
SummaryCOIlength <- unlist(strsplit(summaryCOI[1,1], split = ":", fixed = TRUE))[2]
NumberSequencesCOI2 <- as.numeric(SummaryCOIlength)
all.equal(NumberSequencesCOI1, NumberSequencesCOI2)

𝛉 estimates
Estimate 𝛉 per locus, 𝛉 per site, and 𝛉 variance based on the the number of segregating sites (theta.s) and also estimate 𝛉 per locus based on the number of alleles (theta.k).

# Calculate theta per sequence, theta per site, theta variance from the Watterson estimator based on number of segregating sites.
ThetaCOIperLocusW <- theta.s(sCOI, NumberSequencesCOI1)
ThetaCOIperSiteW <- ThetaCOIperLocusW/seqlengthCOI
ThetaCOIperLocusVarW <- theta.s(sCOI, NumberSequencesCOI1, variance = TRUE)
ThetaCOIperLocusVarW <- ThetaCOIperLocusVarW[2]
ThetaCOIk <- theta.k(n = 132, k = 52)

Tajima’s D and R2 tests
Test for potential deviations from neutrality using Tajima’s D (Tajima 1989) and population growth from the Ramos-Onsins and Roza’s test (Ramos-Onsins and Rozas 2002).

# Tests for neutrality including Tajima's D and Ramos-Onsins and Roza's test
tajimaCOI <- tajima.test(ZosteropsCOI)
R2COI <- R2.test(ZosteropsCOI,B = 10000, theta = ThetaCOIperLocusW, plot = TRUE, quiet = FALSE)

title: Genetic differentiation and biogeographic breaks
text:
Goals
What follows is our workflow for estimating genetic distance and differentiation among East Asian and Philippine Zosterops populations and across biogeographic breaks.

title: Genetic differentiation and biogeographic breaks
text:
Getting started
We are using R version 4.4.2, RStudio version 2024.09.1 for the analysis. Quarto version 1.6.39 for Mac OS was used to document the workflow. Set the working directory in RStudio to one where the .vcf file for the SNPs and a text file defining the population for each sample are available.

title: Genetic differentiation and biogeographic breaks
text:
Data files
This analysis requires the filtered variant call format (VCF) file titled zost.filtered.snps.vcf. Additionally the population of origin and/or taxon assignment will need to be defined for each sample. Taxon and population data for this analysis is in the file titled ZosteropsPOPS_distance.txt. In this file populations are defined in reference to the following combinations of (mostly) allopatric taxa and biogeographic regions. For discussions of biogeographic breaks in Japan and the Ryukyu Islands see Komaki 2021 (Komaki 2021) and McKay 2012 (McKay 2011).

Zosterops japonicus

japonicusKOREA The Korean Peninsula and adjacent islands of the South China Sea and Korean and Tsushima Straits.
japonicusJAPAN The main islands of the Japanese archipelago including Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu.
japonicusRYUKYUn The northern Ryukyu islands of the Osumi group including Yakushima and Tanegashima. Populations with this designation are those in the broader Ryukyu archipelago but north of the biogeographic break known as Watse’s Line
japonicusRYUKYUc The central Ryukyu islands including Amami and Okinawa islands and their adjacent islands between the biogeogrphic breaks
japonicusRYUKYUs The southern-most Ryukyu islands of the Sakishima group including the Miyako Islands, Yaeyama Islands, and Yonaguni island.
japonicusHAWAII Introduced population in the Hawaiian archipelago.

Zosterops meyeni

meyeniLANYU Lanyu island off the east coast fo Taiwan.
meyeniBATAN The Batan Islands of the Philippines including Batan and Sabtang islands.

Zosterops montanus

montanusNORTH The Northern Philippine islands of Luzon and Mindoro.
montanusVISAYAS The Visayas region of the central Philippines including the main islands of Negros, Panay, Cebu, Bohol, Leyte, and Samar.
montanusMINDANAO The southern most islands of the Philippines including the island of Mindanao. Included with Z. montanus samples from Mindanao in this analysis is a Z. nigrorum sample (Zni14341). This sample originating from the island of Camiguin Sur off the northern coast of Mindanao was initially assigned to the Z. nigrorum subspecies catarmanensis but in this study was found to cluster strongly with the central and southern Philippine populations of Z. montanus in both Sanger sequencing and SNP datasets.
montanusINDONESIA The remaining Z. montanus populations of the Indonesian archipelago.

Zosterops simplex

simplexASIA All Z. simplex populations on either the island of Taiwan or on mainland continental Asia.
simplexNA Introduced Z. simplex populations in the southern California region of North America.

Additional outgroup taxa

erythropleurus Z. erythropleurus including samples originating in the breeding range in the Russian Far East and wintering individuals in Southeast Asia.
everetti Z. everetti in the Visayas and Southern Philippines.
nigrorum Z. nigrorum in the Visayas and Northern Philippines.
palpebrosus Z. palpebrosus samples from Vietnam.

title: Genetic differentiation and biogeographic breaks
text:
Distance and population Fst

Packages
Set the working directory to one where the SNP data file zost.filtered.snps.vcf and the taxon/population designation file ZosteropsPOPS_distance.txt are both accessible. Conducting the distance and Fst analysis on these data and generating the associated figures and maps requires the following R packages.

logr (Bosak 2024) Optional if you wish to create a log file for the analysis.
vcfR (Knaus and Grünwald 2017)
SNPfiltR (DeRaad 2023)

Data files
This analysis requires the filtered variant call format (VCF) file titled zost.filtered.snps.vcf. Additionally the population of origin and/or taxon assignment will need to be defined for each sample. Taxon and population data for this analysis is in the file titled ZosteropsPOPS_distance.txt. In this file populations are defined in reference to the following combinations of (mostly) allopatric taxa and biogeographic regions. For discussions of biogeographic breaks in Japan and the Ryukyu Islands see Komaki 2021 (Komaki 2021) and McKay 2012 (McKay 2011).

Zosterops japonicus

japonicusKOREA The Korean Peninsula and adjacent islands of the South China Sea and Korean and Tsushima Straits.
japonicusJAPAN The main islands of the Japanese archipelago including Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu.
japonicusRYUKYUn The northern Ryukyu islands of the Osumi group including Yakushima and Tanegashima. Populations with this designation are those in the broader Ryukyu archipelago but north of the biogeographic break known as Watse’s Line
japonicusRYUKYUc The central Ryukyu islands including Amami and Okinawa islands and their adjacent islands between the biogeogrphic breaks
japonicusRYUKYUs The southern-most Ryukyu islands of the Sakishima group including the Miyako Islands, Yaeyama Islands, and Yonaguni island.
japonicusHAWAII Introduced population in the Hawaiian archipelago.

Zosterops meyeni

meyeniLANYU Lanyu island off the east coast fo Taiwan.
meyeniBATAN The Batan Islands of the Philippines including Batan and Sabtang islands.

Zosterops montanus

montanusNORTH The Northern Philippine islands of Luzon and Mindoro.
montanusVISAYAS The Visayas region of the central Philippines including the main islands of Negros, Panay, Cebu, Bohol, Leyte, and Samar.
montanusMINDANAO The southern most islands of the Philippines including the island of Mindanao. Included with Z. montanus samples from Mindanao in this analysis is a Z. nigrorum sample (Zni14341). This sample originating from the island of Camiguin Sur off the northern coast of Mindanao was initially assigned to the Z. nigrorum subspecies catarmanensis but in this study was found to cluster strongly with the central and southern Philippine populations of Z. montanus in both Sanger sequencing and SNP datasets.
montanusINDONESIA The remaining Z. montanus populations of the Indonesian archipelago.

Zosterops simplex

simplexASIA All Z. simplex populations on either the island of Taiwan or on mainland continental Asia.
simplexNA Introduced Z. simplex populations in the southern California region of North America.

Additional outgroup taxa

erythropleurus Z. erythropleurus including samples originating in the breeding range in the Russian Far East and wintering individuals in Southeast Asia.
everetti Z. everetti in the Visayas and Southern Philippines.
nigrorum Z. nigrorum in the Visayas and Northern Philippines.
palpebrosus Z. palpebrosus samples from Vietnam.

Convert data to Genlight format
Convert the SNP dataset ZosteropsVCF object into a genlight object required for estimating distance and Fst in StAMMP and assign the correct taxa and populations to that object.

ZosteropsGEN <- vcfR2genlight(ZosteropsVCF)
ZosteropsGEN@pop <- as.factor(sample.info$POP)



Estimate Fst and Nei’s distance
Generate the Fst and Nei’s distance estimates from the Zosterops genlight object (ZosteropsGEN).

ZosteropsFST <- stamppFst(ZosteropsGEN, nboots = 100, percent = 95, nclusters = 4)
ZosteropsFSTmatrix <- ZosteropsFST$Fsts
ZosteropsFSTmatrix[upper.tri(ZosteropsFSTmatrix)] <- t(ZosteropsFSTmatrix)[upper.tri(ZosteropsFSTmatrix)]
ZosteropsFSTheat <- reshape::melt(ZosteropsFSTmatrix)

title: StarBEAST2
text:
Goals
What follows is our workflow for the StarBEAST2 analysis for Zosterops. In this analysis we will generate Zosterops species trees from our individual Sanger sequenced loci using Bayesian phylogenetic inference and the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm.

title: StarBEAST2
text:
Getting started
We are using BEAST v2.7.4 for the analysis (R. Bouckaert et al. 2019, 2014; Alexei J. Drummond et al. 2012; Alexei J. Drummond and Rambaut 2007). Quarto version 1.6.39 for Mac OS was used to document the workflow.

title: StarBEAST2
text:
Data files
This analysis requires the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) alignments and the phased nuclear coding DNA (cdDNA) alignments from the Sanger sequenced Zosterops loci. The protocol for phasing the cdDNA alignments may be found in the Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees section. In addition a taxon set file will be required to assign individual samples to their taxon and/or population of origin.
Subsequent analysis requires the following .fasta files including the mtDNA alignments and the phased cdDNA alignments from the procedure described in the Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees section.

COI.fasta
ND2.fasta
B3GNT9_phased.fasta
BIRC2_phased.fasta
CCDC_phased.fasta
GPRC6_phased.fasta
LACTBL_phased.fasta
USP38_phased.fasta

Below are the taxon set files required for these analyses.

Zosterops taxon sets A.txt
Zosterops taxon sets B.txt

title: StarBEAST2
text:
Software and packages
BEAST2 software is available here. This analysis was conducted on a prior version of BEAST2 (v2.7.4 available here) but nearly identical results were achieved using the most recent version of BEAST2 (v2.7.7 as of the writing of this protocol). BEAUTi2 is the tool available with BEAST2 that allows for package management and a graphical user interface (GUI) to generate the .xml files needed to run analyses. The programs LogCombiner and TreeAnnotator are also included with a BEAST2 install and will be needed to process the results of the MCMC runs. In addition the program Tracer will be required to assess the results of an MCMC run and FigTree to edit and visualize species trees produced by BEAST2. Below is a summary of the needed software for this analysis and links to downloads.

BEAST2 v2.7.4 (R. Bouckaert et al. 2019) This install will include BEAST2, BEAUTi2, LogCombiner, and TreeAnnotator.
Tracer (Rambaut et al. 2018)
FigTree

In addition the following packages will need to be installed from the BEAUTi2 GUI using the package manager. To install packages in BEAUTi2 select File from the top bar and Manage Packages from the drop down menu. The package manager will display a table of installed packages and their latest versions. To install select the desired package and click on the Install/Upgrade button. After installing or upgrading packages you will have to close BEAUTi2 and restart before proceeding. Install the following packages.

bModelTest (R. R. Bouckaert and Drummond 2017)
StarBEAST2 (Ogilvie, Bouckaert, and Drummond 2017)

title: StarBEAST2
text:
Generating the .xml file
After installing the needed packages restart BEAUTi2. From the File menu select Template and then StarBeast2. The StarBEAST2 template should display nine tabs titled as follows; Partitions, Taxon Sets, Tip Dates, Gene Ploidy, Population Model, Site Model, Clock Model, Priors, and MCMC.

Partitions
Sequence alignments will be added to the .xml file in the Partitions tab. This can be done by either clicking the + button at the bottom of the tab and selecting Import Alignment from the subsequent menu options or by simply dragging the .fasta file for each alignment into the Partitions tab. After specifying that an alignment is being imported select nucleotide when asked by BEAUTi2 to “Choose the datatype”. For each locus the correct number of taxa, sites, and data type should be listed. For each the file name will be used as the name BEAST2 uses for that particular locus. Also each locus should have a Site Model, Clock Model, and Tree unique to that alignment and with the same name. The Partition tab should look like this when completed.



Taxon sets
For the mtDNA alignments each individual sample has only a single sequence while there are two sequences for the nuclear and therefore diploid cdDNA alignments. The two phased sequences for each diploid individual sample should be labeled a and b (i.e. ZJja004a and ZJja004b are the two phased sequences for sample ZJja004). The a and b suffixes were automatically added to sample names for the phased sequences in PHASE 2.1.1 (see Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees). For consistency an a suffix was manually added to the sample name for each sequence in the mtDNA alignments to prevent a third sample name from appearing for each sample with both mtDNA and cdDNA sequences in the Taxon sets tab.
Click the Taxon sets tab. A list of sample names corresponding to the sequences in the alignments should appear in the Taxon column. For each sample a designation could be manually entered into the Species/Population column (time consuming) or automatically filled from a taxon sets file. To automatically add information on taxon assignment and/or population of origin click the Guess button at the bottom of the tab. Another window will open. Select the radio button corresponding to the read from file and the corresponding Browse button to select the appropriate taxon sets file. For the first set of BEAST2 runs samples were grouped by taxon (species and subspecies) and geography (island or island group) according to the Zosterops taxon sets A.txt file. This file is tab delimited and contains no headers and two columns with the identifying string for each individual sequence and the associated taxon and locality data as follows.

Different sets of StarBEAST2 runs will employ different .xml files each with a different taxon set. Below is what the Taxon sets tab should look like with Zosterops taxon sets A.txt. The first run will be with this taxon set specifying both taxon and geographic localities.



Tip dates
The next tab in BEAUTi2 is the Tip Dates tab. The only selection in this tab is a check box associated with Use tip dates. Leave this box unchecked and proceed to the next tab.



Gene ploidy
The ploidy for each locus is set on the next tab titled, appropriately, Gene Ploidy. A list of loci corresponding to those alignments imported into the Partitions tab should appear in the Gene Ploidy tab. Enter the ploidy for each locus in the corresponding box. Nuclear cdDNA loci are diploid and biparentally inherited so for those loci enter a ploidy of 2.0. The mtDNA loci are uniparentally inherited and haploid. For the mtDNA loci enter 0.5 in the ploidy box. When completed this tab should appear as follows.



Population Model
In the Population Model tab select Analytical Population Size integration from the dropdown menu.



Site Model
Substitution models for each unlinked locus are set in the Site Model tab. For each locus use bModelTest to estimate the best substitution model. If the bModelTest package (see Software and Packages section above) was installed then this option should be available in BEAUTi2 in the dropdown at the top of the Site Model tab as the BEAST Model Test option. For each locus select BEAST Model Test from the dropdown and for Mutation Rate click the estimate box. Mutation rates among loci are estimated relative to one another so leave the Mutation Rate at 1.0 for each locus. Repeat this process for each locus.

title: Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees
text:
Goals
What follows is our workflow for the general descriptive analysis of the Sanger sequencing data set for Zosterops. In this analysis we will describe the variation across our individual Sanger sequenced loci and construct trees for each of these loci using distance-based and maximum likelihood methods.

title: Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees
text:
Getting started
We are using R version 4.4.2, RStudio version 2024.09.1 for the analysis. Quarto version 1.6.39 for Mac OS was used to document the workflow. Set the working directory in RStudio to one where the necessary phased Sanger sequencing alignments and other data are accessible.

title: Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees
text:
Data files
This dataset includes Sanger sequenced polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplicon alignments for two mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and six protein coding nuclear loci (cdDNA). Prior to this analysis Sanger sequencing .ab1 files were uploaded to GeneiousⓇ 8.1.9 for editing, alignment, and quality control. Multiple sequencing runs for each amplicon were assembled and assembled loci were aligned across individual samples using Geneious Alignment. Alignments for each locus were trimmed and edited in Geneious and the identity of each locus confirmed with a megablast search. The reading frame was set by eye by avoiding frames with stop codons and a blastp search was done on the translation consensus for each alignment to confirm the locus identity. Alignments were exported as .fasta files.
Phase alignments of diploid cdDNA loci using PHASE 2.1.1 (Stephens, Smith, and Donnelly 2001). First, convert the alignment .fasta files from Geneious to the .inp format for PHASE 2.1.1 using the online SeqPHASE tool (Flot 2009). At the ‘Genotypes to be phased’ prompt click the ‘Browse’ button and select the appropriate .fasta alignment. Click the ‘Run SeqPHASE’ button. Once step 1 of the SeqPHASE process is completed retain the seqphase.const file in addition to the seqphase.inp file and rename each file appropriately to match the locus name (e.g. B3GNT9_seqphase.inp and B3GNT9_seqphase.const for locus B3GNT9).
Move the .inp from SeqPHASE to the directory with PHASE 2.1.1 and cd to that directory in the terminal. The .inp file is used to run the following PHASE 2.1.1 command in the terminal. For each locus <numberseed> should be replaced with an arbitrary number selected by the user and LOCUSNAME replaced with the designated name for that particular locus. Because each locus is relatively short chose the S option at the modeling flag (-M) as it assumes no within-locus recombination. Additional parameters are explained in the documentation for PHASE 2.1.1 available here.
./PHASE -MS -d1 -S<numberseed> -p0.85 -q0.85 -x5 -X10 LOCUSNAME_seqphase.inp LOCUSNAME_seqphase.out 5000 2 500 
Further analysis will require FASTA alignments for each locus where each diploid individual contains two sequences corresponding to each of the two phased alleles determined in PHASE 2.1.1. Return to the online SeqPHASE tool and click the link to ‘step 2’. Select the appropriate .out file generated by the PHASE 2.1.1 run along with the matching .const file generated from step 1 in the SeqPHASE tool where prompted by a ‘Browse…’ button. The ‘Sort sequence’ box should be checked but the ‘Reduce sequences’ box should not be checked. Click the ‘Run SeqPHASE’ button and SeqPHASE will return a .fasta file with the complete sequence alignment and two phased haplotypes designated by the project number for that individual sample followed by a and b respectively. Click the ‘Click here to download the generated Fasta file’ link at the bottom of the page and rename the file to match the locus name. Including the .const file and unchecking the ‘Reduced sequences’ box will ensure the resulting FASTA file includes the full length of the alignment, not just the variable sites.
The phasing procedure was repeated for the following cdDNA FASTA alignments.

B3GNT9.fasta
BIRC2.fasta
CCDC.fasta
GPRC6.fasta
LACTBL.fasta
USP38.fasta

Subsequent analysis requires the following data files including those phased cdDNA alignments from the procedure described above.

COI.fasta
ND2.fasta
B3GNT9_phased.fasta
BIRC2_phased.fasta
CCDC_phased.fasta
GPRC6_phased.fasta
LACTBL_phased.fasta
USP38_phased.fasta

title: Genetic differentiation and biogeographic breaks
text:
Goals
What follows is our workflow for estimating genetic distance and differentiation among East Asian and Philippine Zosterops populations and across biogeographic breaks.

title: Genetic differentiation and biogeographic breaks
text:
Getting started
We are using R version 4.4.2, RStudio version 2024.09.1 for the analysis. Quarto version 1.6.39 for Mac OS was used to document the workflow. Set the working directory in RStudio to one where the .vcf file for the SNPs and a text file defining the population for each sample are available.

Packages
Set the working directory to one where the SNP data file zost.filtered.snps.vcf and the taxon/population designation file ZosteropsPOPS_distance.txt are both accessible. Conducting the distance and Fst analysis on these data and generating the associated figures and maps requires the following R packages.

logr (Bosak 2024) Optional if you wish to create a log file for the analysis.
vcfR (Knaus and Grünwald 2017)
SNPfiltR (DeRaad 2023)
ggplot2 (Wickham 2016)
adegenet (Jombart 2008)
StAMPP (Pembleton, Cogan, and Forster 2013)
maps (Becker, Minka, and Deckmyn. 2024)
sf (Pebesma and Bivand 2023)
dartR.base (Gruber et al. 2018)

Restart R in the Session/Restart R dropdown in R Studio and create a log file for the analysis (optional).

library(logr)

Data files
This analysis requires the filtered variant call format (VCF) file titled zost.filtered.snps.vcf. Additionally the population of origin and/or taxon assignment will need to be defined for each sample. Taxon and population data for this analysis is in the file titled ZosteropsPOPS_distance.txt. In this file populations are defined in reference to the following combinations of (mostly) allopatric taxa and biogeographic regions. A second taxon assignment file was created assigning individual samples to mostly species designation or more broad allopatric groups within species. That file is titled ZosteropsSPECIES.txt. A detailed description of the assignments in each file is shown below. For discussions of biogeographic breaks in Japan and the Ryukyu Islands see Komaki 2021 (Komaki 2021) and McKay 2012 (McKay 2011).

Population (island and island group) assignments.
Assignment file ZosteropsPOPS_distance.txt

Zosterops japonicus

japonicusKOREA The Korean Peninsula and adjacent islands of the South China Sea and Korean and Tsushima Straits.
japonicusJAPAN The main islands of the Japanese archipelago including Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu.
japonicusRYUKYUn The northern Ryukyu islands of the Osumi group including Yakushima and Tanegashima. Populations with this designation are those in the broader Ryukyu archipelago but north of the biogeographic break known as Watse’s Line.
japonicusRYUKYUc The central Ryukyu islands including Amami and Okinawa islands and their adjacent islands between the biogeogrphic breaks.
japonicusRYUKYUs The southern-most Ryukyu islands of the Sakishima group including the Miyako Islands, Yaeyama Islands, and Yonaguni island.
japonicusIZU Populations of the Z. japonicus stejnegeri subspecies from the Izu Islands (including Niijima, Aogashima, Kozushima, and Miyake) to Chichijiama island in the Ogasawara islands.
japonicusOGASAWARA Populations of the Z. japonicus alani subspecies in the Ogasawara (including Hahajima, Imotojima, Anejima, and Imotojima islands) and Volcano islands (Iwojima).
japonicusHAWAII Introduced population in the Hawaiian archipelago.

Zosterops meyeni

meyeniLANYU Lanyu island off the east coast fo Taiwan.
meyeniBATAN The Batan Islands of the Philippines including Batan and Sabtang islands.

Zosterops montanus

montanusNORTH The Northern Philippine islands of Luzon and Mindoro.
montanusVISAYAS The Visayas region of the central Philippines including the main islands of Negros, Panay, Cebu, Bohol, Leyte, and Samar.
montanusMINDANAO The southern most islands of the Philippines including the island of Mindanao. Included with Z. montanus samples from Mindanao in this analysis is a Z. nigrorum sample (Zni14341). This sample originating from the island of Camiguin Sur off the northern coast of Mindanao was initially assigned to the Z. nigrorum subspecies catarmanensis but in this study was found to cluster strongly with the central and southern Philippine populations of Z. montanus in both Sanger sequencing and SNP datasets.
montanusPALAWAN Philippine Z. montanus population on the island of Palawan.
montanusINDONESIA The remaining Z. montanus populations of the Indonesian archipelago.

Zosterops simplex

simplexASIA All Z. simplex populations on either the island of Taiwan or on mainland continental Asia.
simplexNA Introduced Z. simplex populations in the southern California region of North America.

Additional outgroup taxa

erythropleurus Z. erythropleurus including samples originating in the breeding range in the Russian Far East and wintering individuals in Southeast Asia.
everetti Z. everetti in the Visayas and Southern Philippines.
nigrorum Z. nigrorum in the Visayas and Northern Philippines.
palpebrosus Z. palpebrosus samples from Vietnam.

montanusSOUTH Philippine Z. montanus populations in the Visayas region of the central Philippines including the main islands of Negros, Panay, Cebu, Bohol, Leyte, and Samar and the southern most islands of the Philippines including the island of Mindanao. Included with Z. montanus samples from Mindanao in this analysis is a Z. nigrorum sample (Zni14341), see description in the previous section above.
montanusPALAWAN Philippine Z. montanus population on the island of Palawan.
montanusINDONESIA The remaining Z. montanus populations of the Indonesian archipelago.

Zosterops simplex

simplex All Z. simplex populations on either the island of Taiwan or on mainland continental Asia and introduced Z. simplex populations in the southern California region of North America.

Additional outgroup taxa

erythropleurus Z. erythropleurus including samples originating in the breeding range in the Russian Far East and wintering individuals in Southeast Asia.
everetti Z. everetti in the Visayas and Southern Philippines.
nigrorum Z. nigrorum in the Visayas and Northern Philippines.
palpebrosus Z. palpebrosus samples from Vietnam.

Packages

Data files
This analysis requires the filtered variant call format (VCF) file titled zost.filtered.snps.vcf. Additionally the population of origin and/or taxon assignment will need to be defined for each sample. Taxon and population data for this analysis is in the file titled ZosteropsPOPS_distance.txt. In this file populations are defined in reference to the following combinations of (mostly) allopatric taxa and biogeographic regions. A second taxon assignment file was created assigning individual samples to mostly species designation or more broad allopatric groups within species. That file is titled ZosteropsSPECIES.txt. A detailed description of the assignments in each file is shown below. For discussions of biogeographic breaks in Japan and the Ryukyu Islands see Komaki 2021 (Komaki 2021) and McKay 2012 (McKay 2011).

Population (island and island group) assignments.
Assignment file ZosteropsPOPS_distance.txt

Zosterops japonicus

japonicusKOREA The Korean Peninsula and adjacent islands of the South China Sea and Korean and Tsushima Straits.
japonicusJAPAN The main islands of the Japanese archipelago including Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu.
japonicusRYUKYUn The northern Ryukyu islands of the Osumi group including Yakushima and Tanegashima. Populations with this designation are those in the broader Ryukyu archipelago but north of the biogeographic break known as Watse’s Line.
japonicusRYUKYUc The central Ryukyu islands including Amami and Okinawa islands and their adjacent islands between the biogeogrphic breaks.
japonicusRYUKYUs The southern-most Ryukyu islands of the Sakishima group including the Miyako Islands, Yaeyama Islands, and Yonaguni island.
japonicusIZU Populations of the Z. japonicus stejnegeri subspecies from the Izu Islands (including Niijima, Aogashima, Kozushima, and Miyake) to Chichijiama island in the Ogasawara islands.
japonicusOGASAWARA Populations of the Z. japonicus alani subspecies in the Ogasawara (including Hahajima, Imotojima, Anejima, and Imotojima islands) and Volcano islands (Iwojima).
japonicusHAWAII Introduced population in the Hawaiian archipelago.

Zosterops meyeni

meyeniLANYU Lanyu island off the east coast fo Taiwan.
meyeniBATAN The Batan Islands of the Philippines including Batan and Sabtang islands.

Zosterops montanus

montanusNORTH The Northern Philippine islands of Luzon and Mindoro.
montanusVISAYAS The Visayas region of the central Philippines including the main islands of Negros, Panay, Cebu, Bohol, Leyte, and Samar.
montanusMINDANAO The southern most islands of the Philippines including the island of Mindanao. Included with Z. montanus samples from Mindanao in this analysis is a Z. nigrorum sample (Zni14341). This sample originating from the island of Camiguin Sur off the northern coast of Mindanao was initially assigned to the Z. nigrorum subspecies catarmanensis but in this study was found to cluster strongly with the central and southern Philippine populations of Z. montanus in both Sanger sequencing and SNP datasets.
montanusPALAWAN Philippine Z. montanus population on the island of Palawan.
montanusINDONESIA The remaining Z. montanus populations of the Indonesian archipelago.

Zosterops simplex

simplexASIA All Z. simplex populations on either the island of Taiwan or on mainland continental Asia.
simplexNA Introduced Z. simplex populations in the southern California region of North America.

Additional outgroup taxa

erythropleurus Z. erythropleurus including samples originating in the breeding range in the Russian Far East and wintering individuals in Southeast Asia.
everetti Z. everetti in the Visayas and Southern Philippines.
nigrorum Z. nigrorum in the Visayas and Northern Philippines.
palpebrosus Z. palpebrosus samples from Vietnam.

title: StarBEAST2
text:
Goals
What follows is our workflow for the StarBEAST2 analysis for Zosterops. In this analysis we will generate Zosterops species trees from our individual Sanger sequenced loci using Bayesian phylogenetic inference and the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm.

title: StarBEAST2
text:
Getting started
We are using BEAST v2.7.4 for the analysis (R. Bouckaert et al. 2019, 2014; Alexei J. Drummond et al. 2012; Alexei J. Drummond and Rambaut 2007). Quarto version 1.6.39 for Mac OS was used to document the workflow.

title: StarBEAST2
text:
Data files
This analysis requires the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) alignments and the phased nuclear coding DNA (cdDNA) alignments from the Sanger sequenced Zosterops loci. The protocol for phasing the cdDNA alignments may be found in the Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees section. In addition a taxon set file will be required to assign individual samples to their taxon and/or population of origin.
Subsequent analysis requires the following .fasta files including the mtDNA alignments and the phased cdDNA alignments from the procedure described in the Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees section.

COI.fasta
ND2.fasta
B3GNT9_phased.fasta
BIRC2_phased.fasta
CCDC_phased.fasta
GPRC6_phased.fasta
LACTBL_phased.fasta
USP38_phased.fasta

Below are the taxon set files required for these analyses.

Zosterops taxon sets A.txt
Zosterops taxon sets B.txt

title: StarBEAST2
text:
Software and packages
BEAST2 software is available here. This analysis was conducted on a prior version of BEAST2 (v2.7.4 available here) but nearly identical results were achieved using the most recent version of BEAST2 (v2.7.7 as of the writing of this protocol). BEAUTi2 is the tool available with BEAST2 that allows for package management and a graphical user interface (GUI) to generate the .xml files needed to run analyses. The programs LogCombiner and TreeAnnotator are also included with a BEAST2 install and will be needed to process the results of the MCMC runs. In addition the program Tracer will be required to assess the results of an MCMC run and FigTree to edit and visualize species trees produced by BEAST2. Below is a summary of the needed software for this analysis and links to downloads.

BEAST2 v2.7.4 (R. Bouckaert et al. 2019) This install will include BEAST2, BEAUTi2, LogCombiner, and TreeAnnotator.
Tracer (Rambaut et al. 2018)
FigTree

In addition the following packages will need to be installed from the BEAUTi2 GUI using the package manager. To install packages in BEAUTi2 select File from the top bar and Manage Packages from the drop down menu. The package manager will display a table of installed packages and their latest versions. To install select the desired package and click on the Install/Upgrade button. After installing or upgrading packages you will have to close BEAUTi2 and restart before proceeding. Install the following packages.

bModelTest (R. R. Bouckaert and Drummond 2017)
StarBEAST2 (Ogilvie, Bouckaert, and Drummond 2017)

title: StarBEAST2
text:
Generating the .xml file
After installing the needed packages restart BEAUTi2. From the File menu select Template and then StarBeast2. The StarBEAST2 template should display nine tabs titled as follows; Partitions, Taxon Sets, Tip Dates, Gene Ploidy, Population Model, Site Model, Clock Model, Priors, and MCMC.

Partitions
Sequence alignments will be added to the .xml file in the Partitions tab. This can be done by either clicking the + button at the bottom of the tab and selecting Import Alignment from the subsequent menu options or by simply dragging the .fasta file for each alignment into the Partitions tab. After specifying that an alignment is being imported select nucleotide when asked by BEAUTi2 to “Choose the datatype”. For each locus the correct number of taxa, sites, and data type should be listed. For each the file name will be used as the name BEAST2 uses for that particular locus. Also each locus should have a Site Model, Clock Model, and Tree unique to that alignment and with the same name. The Partition tab should look like this when completed.



Taxon sets
For the mtDNA alignments each individual sample has only a single sequence while there are two sequences for the nuclear and therefore diploid cdDNA alignments. The two phased sequences for each diploid individual sample should be labeled a and b (i.e. ZJja004a and ZJja004b are the two phased sequences for sample ZJja004). The a and b suffixes were automatically added to sample names for the phased sequences in PHASE 2.1.1 (see Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees). For consistency an a suffix was manually added to the sample name for each sequence in the mtDNA alignments to prevent a third sample name from appearing for each sample with both mtDNA and cdDNA sequences in the Taxon sets tab.
Click the Taxon sets tab. A list of sample names corresponding to the sequences in the alignments should appear in the Taxon column. For each sample a designation could be manually entered into the Species/Population column (time consuming) or automatically filled from a taxon sets file. To automatically add information on taxon assignment and/or population of origin click the Guess button at the bottom of the tab. Another window will open. Select the radio button corresponding to the read from file and the corresponding Browse button to select the appropriate taxon sets file. Click the Show options button and select txt to allow for the selection of .txt files as taxon set entries. For the first set of BEAST2 runs samples were grouped by taxon (species and subspecies) and geography (island or island group) according to the Zosterops taxon sets A.txt file. This file is tab delimited and contains no headers and two columns with the identifying string for each individual sequence and the associated taxon and locality data as follows.

Different sets of StarBEAST2 runs will employ different .xml files each with a different taxon set. Below is what the Taxon sets tab should look like with Zosterops taxon sets A.txt. The first run will be with this taxon set specifying both taxon and geographic localities.



Tip dates
The next tab in BEAUTi2 is the Tip Dates tab. The only selection in this tab is a check box associated with Use tip dates. Leave this box unchecked and proceed to the next tab.



Gene ploidy
The ploidy for each locus is set on the next tab titled, appropriately, Gene Ploidy. A list of loci corresponding to those alignments imported into the Partitions tab should appear in the Gene Ploidy tab. Enter the ploidy for each locus in the corresponding box. Nuclear cdDNA loci are diploid and biparentally inherited so for those loci enter a ploidy of 2.0. The mtDNA loci are uniparentally inherited and haploid. For the mtDNA loci enter 0.5 in the ploidy box. When completed this tab should appear as follows.



Population Model
In the Population Model tab select Analytical Population Size integration from the dropdown menu.



Site Model
Substitution models for each unlinked locus are set in the Site Model tab. For each locus use bModelTest to estimate the best substitution model. If the bModelTest package (see Software and Packages section above) was installed then this option should be available in BEAUTi2 in the dropdown at the top of the Site Model tab as the BEAST Model Test option. For each locus select BEAST Model Test from the dropdown and for Mutation Rate click the estimate box. Mutation rates among loci are estimated relative to one another so leave the Mutation Rate at 1.0 for each locus. Repeat this process for each locus.



Clock Model
Next set the molecular clock model. Click on the Clock Model tab. For each locus added to the Partition tab there should be a corresponding entry listed in the Clock Model tab. For all loci select Strict Clock from the drop down menu at the top of the tab. The substitution rate for mtDNA was based on a divergence rate of 2.1% per million years (Ma). This equates to a mean of 1.05% or 0.0105 substitutions/site/lineage/Ma. This range is consistent with mtDNA substitution rates reported in birds (FLEISCHER, MCINTOSH, and TARR 1998; Pereira and Baker 2006; WEIR and SCHLUTER 2008; Eo and DeWoody 2010). For both the mtDNA loci (COI and ND2) enter 0.0105 in the Clock.rate box and click the estimate box. Nuclear cdDNA were assumed to have a significantly lower substitution rate. For the cdDNA loci enter 0.00105 in the Clock.rate boxes and check the estimate box.



Priors
StarBEAST2 is a Bayesian method and as such it requires the user to set the priors for various parameters. For these analyses the default priors will be used for everything except for the clock rates. As we did for the Clock Model tab clock rate priors will be based off of molecular clock rates estimated in the literature. Click on the Priors tab and scroll down to the strictClockRate values for each locus. Select the arrow symbol on the left to reveal the settings for the strictClockRate prior distribution for each locus. A LogNormal distribution from the drop down menu should be selected for all the strictClockRate priors. The box to the right should have the initial clock rate for each locus (same as defined in the Clock Rate tab) and show lower and upper bounds from 0.0 to infinity. Consistent with mtDNA substitution rates reported in birds (FLEISCHER, MCINTOSH, and TARR 1998; Pereira and Baker 2006; WEIR and SCHLUTER 2008; Eo and DeWoody 2010) the mean clock rate (M) for the mtDNA loci (COI and ND2) will be set at 0.0105 substitutions/site/lineage/Ma with a standard deviation (S) of 1.0. Make sure the Mean in Real Space box is checked to view the prior distribution. For the mtDNA loci M = 0.0105 and S = 1.0 and a log normal distribution results in a 5 - 95% quantile range of 0.00123 - 0.033 and a median clock rate of 0.00637. The same conditions should be set for each of the cdDNA locus priors except that the mean (M) should be set at 1/10th the clock rate of the mtDNA loci (M = 0.00105). For the cdDNA loci the 5 - 95% quantile range is 0.000123 - 0.0033 and the median clock rate is 0.000637.



MCMC
The final tab (MCMC) sets the parameters for the run. Enter 10 million (10000000) in the Chain Length box. Enter 20000 in the box titled Store Every to indicate that results should be stored every 20,000 iteration of the MCMC chain. The burnin period should be 1 million. Enter 1000000 into the corresponding Pre Burnin box. The number of initiation attempts should be 10 (enter 10 for the Num Initiation Attempts box). Leave the remaining parameters at their default values.



Save .xml file
All the needed parameters for the .xml file are now completed. Save the file by selecting File from the top bar in BEAUTi2 and Save as. Replicate multiple independent runs in three groups. Group A uses the Zosterops taxon sets A.txt file in the .xml setup with both taxon and island information to define the individual samples. Group B also uses both taxon and island information in the BEAUTi2 Taxon sets tab during the .xml setup but employs the Zosterops taxon sets mtDNA.txt file to define the individual samples. Group A .xml files include all loci in the Partitions tab. Group B .xml files include only the two mtDNA loci (COI and ND2) in the Partitions tab. Group C runs include all loci in the Partitions tab but use the Zosterops taxon sets B.txt file to define the samples by taxon only, collapsing populations across multiple localities into the same taxonomic group. Create a working directory for each run labeled appropriately (A1-20; B1-20; C1-20). Create one .xml file for each of these groups and duplicate that file 20 times changing the file name to create a sequential series of .xml files from 1 -20 (A1-A20 for Group A, B1-B20 for Group B, and C1-C20 for group C).
Names for .xml files for the first runs in each group are as follows. STARBEAST274 denotes the version of StarBeast2 used and BMT denotes that these runs use bModelTest for the site model selection.
Zosterops_STARBEAST274BMT_A1.xml
Zosterops_STARBEAST274BMT_B1.xml
Zosterops_STARBEAST274BMT_C1.xml

title: StarBEAST2
text:
MCMC BEAST2 Runs
There will be three sets of 20 MCMC runs for this analysis. For each run follow these instructions. Create a separate directory for each run labeled A1 - A20 for the Group A runs, B1 - B20 for the Group B runs, and C1 - C20 for the Group C runs. Each directory should contain the appropriate .xml file created in BEAUTi2. Open BEAST2. The following dialog window should appear. Use the Choose file… button to select the appropriate .xml file for the run. A different value should appear in the Random number seed box with each separate run. If your machine will allow it increase the number of threads and instances. Our runs were executed on either an Apple M1 iMac with 16GB RAM or an Apple M2 Max MacBook Pro with 96GB RAM with 20 threads and 4 instances. Click the Run button. Once BEAST2 is running the dialog window may be closed and the progress of the run monitored. Each run on either of these machines took approximately 30 minutes.

title: StarBEAST2
text:
Combining log and tree files
For each of the run groups (A, B, and C) combine the .log and the .tree files generated by BEAST and saved in the run directory. Open the LogCombiner application included with the BEAST2 download. For File type select Log Files from the dropdown. Drag and drop all the .log files from StarBEAST2 runs within a group into the Select input files box. Click the Choose file… button and at the prompt name the combined .log file. Combined .log files for the three groups of StarBEAST2 runs are as follows.
ZosteropsStarbeastCombinedA.log
ZosteropsStarbeastCombinedB.log
ZosteropsStarbeastCombinedC.log
Repeat the same process for the species .tree files for the three run groups (A, B, and C). Combine the species trees from each run and not the individual locus trees. Open the LogCombiner application included with the BEAST2 download and select Tree Files from the File Type drop down. Drag and drop all the species .tree files from StarBEAST2 runs within a group into the Select input files box. Click the Choose file… button and at the prompt name the combined .tree file. Combined .tree files for the three groups of StarBEAST2 runs are as follows.
ZosteropsSpeciesCombinedA.trees
ZosteropsSpeciesCombinedB.trees
ZosteropsSpeciesCombinedC.trees

title: StarBEAST2
text:
Maximum clade credibility consensus tree
Open the TreeAnnotator application included with the BEAST2 download. Enter 10 for the Burn in percentage. Leave the Posterior probability limit at 0.0. Choose Maximum clade credibility tree from the drop down menu for Target tree type and Common Ancestor heights for the Node heights. Select the combined species tree file from the previous step by clicking the Choose file… button at the Input Tree File prompt. For the Output File selection click the Choose file… button and name the file and choose the appropriate directory. Consensus species tree files are named as follows.
ZosteropsSpeciesA.trees
ZosteropsSpeciesB.trees
ZosteropsSpeciesC.trees

title: BPP and GDI based species delimitation
text: What follows is our workflow for the Bayesian Phylogenetics and Phylogeography (BP&P or hereafter just BPP) and genealogical diversity index (GDI) analyses for East Asian Zosterops. Using the multispecies coalescent (Flouri et al. 2019), the BPP software package v4.7.0 (Flouri et al. 2018), and the GDI hueristic species delimitation methods outlined in Leaché et al. 2019 (Leaché et al. 2018) this analysis attempts to estimate 𝜃 and test species hypotheses against the eight locus Sanger sequencing dataset for East Asian Zosterops (see Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees section).

title: BPP and GDI based species delimitation
text:
Goals
What follows is our workflow for the Bayesian Phylogenetics and Phylogeography (BP&P or hereafter just BPP) and genealogical diversity index (GDI) analyses for East Asian Zosterops. Using the multispecies coalescent (Flouri et al. 2019), the BPP software package v4.7.0 (Flouri et al. 2018), and the GDI hueristic species delimitation methods outlined in Leaché et al. 2019 (Leaché et al. 2018) this analysis attempts to estimate 𝜃 and test species hypotheses against the eight locus Sanger sequencing dataset for East Asian Zosterops (see Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees section).

title: BPP and GDI based species delimitation
text:
Getting started
We are using R version 4.4.2 and RStudio version 2024.09.1 to illustrate the guide trees in for BPP, calculate GDI, and plot 𝜃 and GDI. Quarto version 1.6.39 for Mac OS was used to document the workflow. The analysis was conducted using BPP v4.7.0. The BPP manual is an excellent introduction to these analyses.

title: BPP and GDI based species delimitation
text:
Data files

Sequence alignments
The data used for this analysis will be restricted to those Sanger sequences from Zosterops japonicus, Z. meyeni, Z. montanus, and Z. simplex. The sequence file is in phylip format.
To illustrate the data format an excerpt of the sequence file ZosteropsBPP_JMMSseq.txt is shown below (ellipsis indicates where additional sequences from the original file have been left out). One alignment of individual sequences follows the other sequentially in a single file. A space followed by two numbers initiate the beginning of a locus. First is the number of individual sequences for that locus. Remember that for those loci from phased nuclear coding DNA (cdDNA) there will be two sequences for each individual with the individual identifying code followed by a and b to denote the two phased alleles (see Sanger sequencing summary statistics and trees section). Each sequence will lead with the sample, an a for the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) loci or either a or b for the phased cdDNA loci, and underscore, the locus name (e.g. COI, ND2, B3GNT9), a ^ symbol, and finally the individual sample name (minus the allelic designations, a and/or b). Taxon maps and guide trees
The final data file needed for these analyses is an imap file saved in .txt format that maps the taxon and/or population designations to individual samples. Individual samples in the imap file should match those in the phylip formatted sequence file. Four imap files will be needed for the analysis.

ZosteropsBPPtip_imap.txt
ZosteropsBPPmid1_imap.txt
ZosteropsBPPmid2_imap.txt
ZosteropsBPProot_imap.txt

Codes in these files are designated for each taxon as follows.

Jp - Z. japonicus
Me - Z. meyeni
MoN - Z. montanus Northern Philippines including subspecies halconensis (Mindoro) and whiteheadi (Luzon)
MoS - Z. montanus Southern Philippines, Palawan, and Indonesia including subspecies Z. montanus diuatae (Mindanao), Z. montanus vulcani (Mindanao), Z. montanus pectoralis (Negros), Z. montanus parkesi (Palawan), Z. montanus montanus (Indonesia), and an unnamed Z. montanus population on the Philippine island of Panay.
Si - Z. simplex including populations on the island of Taiwan and Mainland Asia.



Trees

TIP tree
This topology is derived from the single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) dataset analyzed in the Singular Value Decomposition Quartets (SVDQ) package (see SVDQ and QAGE section) and the Sanger sequencing dataset analyzed in BEAST2 (see Star BEAST2 section). Branches are color coded here to match the corresponding density distributions in subsequent analyses. Each tree collapses taxa so BPP analyses may estimate 𝜃 and 𝜏 along each branch.

TIP <- read.tree(text = '((((Jp,Me),MoN),MoS),Si);')
edge_colors <- c("#EEA2AD", "#1E90FF", "#FF8C00", "#D82632", "#FED439", "#B66DFF", "#FA9C88", "#008600")
plot(TIP, edge.color = edge_colors[1:length(TIP$edge)], edge.width = 4, label.offset = 0.1)
nodes <- c("A", "B", "C", "D")
nodelabels(nodes)
edgelabels()










MID1 tree
Collapses the Z. japonicus and Z. meyeni branches.

MID1 <- read.tree(text = '(((JpMe,MoN),MoS),Si);')
plot(MID1, edge.width = 4, label.offset = 0.1)










MID2 tree
Collapses the Z. japonicus/Z. meyeni branch and Z. montanus from the Northern Philippines.

MID2 <- read.tree(text = '((JpMeMoN,MoS),Si);')
plot(MID2, edge.width = 4, label.offset = 0.1)










ROOT tree
Collapses Z. japonicus, Z. meyeni, Z. motanus in the Northern Philippines, and Z. montanus in Indonesia and the Southern Philippines into a single branch connected to the outgroup (Z. simplex) by a single node.

ROOT <- read.tree(text = '(JpMeMoNMoS,Si);')
plot(ROOT, edge.width = 4, label.offset = 0.1)

title: BPP and GDI based species delimitation
text:
Genealogical diversity index (GDI)
\(2\tau/\theta_A\) is the population divergence time for population \(A\) in coalescent units. One coalescent unit is equal to \(2N_A\) generations where \(N_A\) is the effective population size of \(A\). \(e^{(-2\tau/\theta_A)}\) is the probability that two sequences (\(a_1\) and \(a_2\)) from population \(A\) fail to coalesce before the divergence (𝜏) of \(A\) from its sister lineage. The GDI is the complementary probability of \(e^{(-2\tau/\theta_A)}\) and reflects the probability that \(a_1\) and \(a_2\) do coalesce prior to (going backwards in time) the divergence between population \(A\) and its sister lineage (𝜏) . GDI therefore may be calculated from 𝜃 and 𝜏 using the following equation (Jackson et al. 2016; Leaché et al. 2018).
\[
GDI = 1 - e^{(-2\tau/\theta_A)}
\]
The BPP A00 analyses will estimate 𝜃 and 𝜏 along each branch in a given tree and we then use those values to calculate the GDI for each branch.

# A RUNS are BPP runs under the A10 conditions with species delimitation under a fixed tree.
# B-E RUNS are BPP runs under the A00 conditions with no species delimitation and a fixed tree.
# Each set of runs are done under three replicates, four imap files corresponding to different branches of the tree (tip, mid1, mid2, root), and four different combinations of theta and tau prior distributions.
# Taxon codes for trees: Jp (Z. japonicus), Me (Z. meyeni), MoN (Northern Philippine Z. montanus on Luzon and Mindoror), MoS (Southern Philippine Z. montanus in the Visayas and Mindanao), Si (outgroup, Z. simplex on Mainland Asia and Taiwan)
# Trees for .ctl files...
  # B RUNS Tip ((((Jp, Me), MoN), MoS), Si)
  # C RUNS Mid1 (((JpMe, MoN), MoS), Si)
  # D RUNS Mid2 ((JpMeMoN, MoS), Si)
  # E RUNS Root (JpMeMoNMoS, Si)
# Beta values for Theta and Tau...
  # Z1 0.001 0.004  Z2 0.002 0.004  Z3 0.001 0.000  Z4 0.002 0.0005
  # Tip B1-3 0.001 0.004 B4-6 0.002 0.004 B7-9 0.001 0.0005 B10-12 0.002 0.0005
  # Mid1 C1-3 0.001 0.004 C4-6 0.002 0.004 C7-9 0.001 0.0005 C10-12 0.002 0.0005
  # Mid2 D1-3 0.001 0.004 D4-6 0.002 0.004 D7-9 0.001 0.0005 D10-12 0.002 0.0005
  # Root E1-3 0.001 0.004 E4-6 0.002 0.004 E7-9 0.001 0.0005 E10-12 0.002 0.0005
